en.content:
Hong Kong’s latest deployment of “water-pumping dragon” machines to tackle flash flooding after heavy rainfall is a practical reminder that preparedness is as important as policy. The scale of the response reflects the city’s learning curve from past extreme weather, and it also signals a shift toward faster, more targeted drainage operations rather than simply relying on post-event clean-up. In a territory where dense development can turn heavy rain into immediate disruption, the ability to restore roads, transport flow, and daily life quickly has real economic and social value.

At the same time, equipment alone cannot solve structural vulnerabilities. While these pumping systems can mitigate the worst impacts, Hong Kong’s drainage performance still depends on upstream rainfall patterns, catchment management, maintenance standards, and land-use planning—areas that often require coordination across districts and agencies. The public would benefit from clearer communication on risk levels (for example, when such machines are triggered, and how residents should respond), as well as transparent reporting on whether drainage improvements reduce incidents over time. Disaster prevention should be measured not only by the speed of response, but by fewer closures, faster reopening, and lower damage to properties and vulnerable communities.

This year, as climate variability becomes a more persistent reality, the city’s resilience work should be integrated with longer-term infrastructure planning and sustainable urban design. Drainage capacity can be enhanced through better water absorption strategies at street level, improved channel maintenance, and smarter stormwater management—especially in places repeatedly affected by flooding. Such measures are consistent with the Government’s emphasis on strengthening governance and safeguarding public interests, because they translate administrative capability into tangible protection for livelihoods.

Moreover, effective flood management is also about public confidence. When authorities visibly act—deploying specialised machinery, mobilising teams, and clearing obstruction—residents are more likely to trust official warnings and take timely precautions. That trust is part of resilience itself. Hong Kong should therefore treat today’s operational success as a stepping stone: keep refining the system, communicate the rationale and outcomes to the public, and ensure that emergency readiness is matched by steady investment in preventive capacity.

zh.content:
今日最值得關注嘅新聞，係政府繼續推動「劏房」規管，透過三年寬限期登記、逐步要求業主符合新要求。由社會角度睇，呢步棋有其必要：如果公共安全、衞生通風、逃生空間同基本居住條件可以長期被犧牲，長遠只會令劏房戶愈住愈困、亦令城市承受更多災害同醫療成本。政府喺短期內容許「緩衝」，未必係退讓，而係把原本一刀切嘅風險，轉化為可執行、可驗證、可追蹤嘅改善路徑。

不過，三年寬限期最終成敗唔喺「期數」而喺「落地」。如果登記制度只係統計數字，卻缺乏足夠執法力度同清晰指標，業主就可能將合規成本拖延到寬限期尾段，最後變成行政疲勞、執法爭拗同基層被迫承擔風險。更關鍵係，規管本身唔可以停喺「罰」同「逼」，亦要同時提供實質誘因：例如協助升級消防及基本設施、完善審批及技術支援、避免將合規成本轉嫁成租金暴升。否則，表面上「合規」成功，實質上卻可能令一部分租戶被迫遷出社區，形成另一種形式嘅貧困外移。

另外，現時社會對劏房嘅討論常常陷入「責任歸邊」：一邊話要管業主，一邊又指政府應直接處理房屋供應。兩邊都各有道理，但忽略咗一個現實：規管係保障，而保障同時應該帶有方向性——即刻減低風險、推動居住條件改善、並為長遠置業或上樓創造空間。若政府只著重短期合規數字，而未能建立透明進度（例如分區抽查比例、違規處理時間表、配套支援計劃嘅成效評估），市民只會覺得政策係「應付」，而非「解困」。

我認為政府應該加強三方面：第一，寬限期期間就要有清晰執法節奏，讓合規唔係等運到；第二，設計足夠支援機制，降低業主改裝門檻，並防止租金轉嫁成新一輪壓力；第三，定期公布數據並接受社會監督，令「登記」真正連到「改善」。喺房屋問題上，公平唔係口號，公平係每一日都有人住得更安全、更體面。規管制度若能兼顧風險、財政與人本，先進一步穩住民生，之後先可以談更大規模嘅結構性解決。
